title: The Middle-Length Sayings
hook: 152 discourses of middle length; we read highlights in order, with Chalmers' translation

segments.voice: Yesterday: the path, and your line, eight together. How many of the eight did you find in one ordinary task? Day four hundred one, and a new block begins.

Some books you read cover to cover. Some you live in. For the next hundred and twenty-one days, we're going to live in one: the Majjhima Nikaya, the Middle-Length Sayings of the Buddha. Not every page, but its highlights, in order. Here's some of what's coming. A man who sits alone in a forest at night until fear arrives. A raft. A saw. A water snake. A murderer who becomes a monk. A man shot with a poisoned arrow who won't let the doctor touch it until he knows who fired it. Today: the book itself.
screen: `A BOOK TO LIVE IN.` → `A RAFT, A SAW, A WATER SNAKE.` → `THE POISONED ARROW.`

segments.voice: Nikaya means a collection, a group. Majjhima means middle. The discourse basket of the Pali canon holds five nikayas, sorted partly by length: the Long Discourses, the Middle-Length, the Connected, the Numbered, and a collection of shorter books. The middle one holds a hundred and fifty-two discourses, longer than a page and shorter than a chapter, arranged in three sets of fifty, with fifty-two in the last. Who's speaking? Mostly the Buddha, but not only. Sariputta teaches. Mahakaccana unpacks a riddle. The nun Dhammadinna answers hard questions. Kings, brahmins, Jain ascetics and wandering philosophers all walk through, and a murderer named Angulimala. Many of the best-known teachings live here: the foundations of mindfulness in MN 10, the raft in MN 22, the noble search in MN 26, the poisoned arrow in MN 63, Angulimala in MN 86. Tradition says these discourses were recited together after the Buddha's death and carried for centuries by memory, by monks who specialized in chanting particular collections, before being written down in Sri Lanka around the first century BCE. In English, a translation by Lord Chalmers, Further Dialogues of the Buddha, appeared in the 1920s; we'll lean on it and on the Pali, mostly in our own retelling. One more thing you'll notice. This book has the feel of a real world. People argue. People misunderstand. Some walk away unconvinced. Not every discourse ends with everyone nodding, and the reciters kept those too.
screen: `NIKAYA — A COLLECTION.` · `152 DISCOURSES, THREE FIFTIES.` · `SARIPUTTA, KINGS, A NUN, A MURDERER.` · `CARRIED BY MEMORY, WRITTEN LATER.` · then, large: `THE MIDDLE LENGTH.`

segments.voice: If you have the list of titles nearby, in a book or on a page, read down it slowly. If not, take these: the root of all things. All the taints. Heirs in the teaching. Fear and dread. The simile of the cloth. The simile of the saw. The water snake. The anthill. Let one title catch you, and don't ask why. Then put the list down, rest with the breath, and let that one title sit beside you. The bell holds the time.
Majjhima Nikaya. The Middle-Length Sayings: a hundred and fifty-two discourses, our book for the next stretch of the path.
Your line: the middle length. Today, read one thing of middle length all the way through, a long article, a letter, a chapter, without skimming. Day four hundred one.

howItsDone: In Theravada countries the Majjhima Nikaya is studied in monasteries and recited in Pali, and many lay Buddhists read it in translation; its suttas are often the texts teachers return to for instruction.

fork.setup: you're a monk a century after the Buddha. there are no written books of his teaching. how do the discourses survive?
options: monks memorize and chant them, collection by collection
each monk writes his own version
fork.reveal: tradition says reciters specialized in particular collections and chanted them together, generation after generation, until they were written down.

original.note: Pali majjhima-nikāya: the middle collection, the Middle-Length Sayings.

trapdoor: what you thought: a medium-sized book of sayings.
what it means: the middle collection of the Pali discourses, 152 suttas, our text for the next 121 days.

what a scholar hears: the three sets of fifty are called paṇṇāsa, 'fifties', each divided into chapters (vagga) of about ten; later commentaries mention reciters called majjhima-bhāṇakas who specialized in this collection.

sources.ref: Lord Chalmers, Further Dialogues of the Buddha (1926–27)
